author: Justin Martyr
occasion: Justin writes after recent unjust actions against Christians under the urban prefect Urbicus in Rome, including a Christian woman, Ptolemy, Lucius, and a third unnamed Christian, to protest irrational persecution and to ask the Roman authorities to publish his defense so others may learn the truth.
argument: Justin protests the irrational persecution of Christians, illustrated by the case of a Christian woman who separated from her unchaste husband, leading to the condemnation of Ptolemy, Lucius, and a third Christian under Urbicus. He explains why Christians do not commit suicide and why they confess fearlessly, attributing persecution to fallen angels and demons who enslave humanity. He argues that Christ is the whole divine Word, of whom all earlier philosophers and lawgivers possessed only a seed, and that Christians therefore possess the fullest truth. He asks the Roman authorities to publish this defense so that people may be freed from false opinion and ignorance.

outline.move: Justin states his purpose: recent unjust actions under Urbicus and elsewhere compel him to write on behalf of the Romans, who share the same human nature.

He narrates the case of a Christian woman who separated from her unchaste husband; the husband first accused her of being a Christian, then turned against Ptolemy, her Christian teacher, leading to the executions of Ptolemy, Lucius, and a third Christian under Urbicus.
He explains why Christians do not kill themselves and why they confess without fear when examined.
He describes how fallen angels fathered demons, enslaved humanity, and caused the evils attributed by poets to the gods.
He discusses the namelessness of the Father, the titles of the Son, and the power of Jesus' name in exorcisms.
He argues that God delays the world's destruction because of the Christian seed, and defends free will against Stoic fate.
He says demons hate all who live by reason, especially Christians who know the whole Word, Christ.
He expects to be plotted against, especially by Crescens, and challenges Crescens to a public examination.
He answers the objection that Christians teach punishment only to frighten people, and defends the reality of virtue and vice.
He argues that Christianity surpasses all human teaching because Christ is the whole Word, of whom Socrates and others knew only a part.
He explains that Christians accept death as a debt owed to God, and contrasts virtue and vice using Xenophon's story of Heracles.
He recounts his own conversion from Platonism and refutes the slanders that Christians commit the crimes attributed to the gods.
He confesses he is a Christian and argues that whatever was said well by any writer belongs to Christians, because all shared in the seed of the Word.
He asks the Romans to publish this book if it seems good to them, so that others may know their teachings and be freed from false opinion and ignorance of good things.
He concludes by affirming that Christian teachings are not shameful but surpass all human philosophy, and prays that all may attain the truth.

cast.name: Justin
cast.who: The author, a Christian philosopher and former Platonist, writing in Rome.

cast.name: Urbicus
cast.who: The Roman urban prefect who condemned Ptolemy, Lucius, and another Christian.

cast.name: Ptolemy
cast.who: A Christian teacher arrested and executed after confessing he was a Christian.

cast.name: Lucius
cast.who: A Christian who protested Ptolemy's unjust condemnation and was himself executed.

cast.name: The Christian woman
cast.who: An unnamed Christian woman who converted from unchastity, separated from her husband by repudium, and was accused by him.

cast.name: The husband
cast.who: The woman's unnamed husband, who continued in vice, accused his wife of being a Christian, and instigated the arrest of Ptolemy.

cast.name: The centurion
cast.who: A centurion, friend of the husband, who arrested and interrogated Ptolemy.

cast.name: Crescens
cast.who: A Cynic philosopher in Rome who publicly slandered Christians; Justin challenges him to a debate.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.who: Athenian philosopher cited as one who knew the Word in part and was persecuted like Christians.

cast.name: Heracles
cast.who: Hero in Xenophon's story who chose between virtue and vice.

cast.name: Xenophon
cast.who: Greek writer who told the story of Heracles at the crossroads.

cast.name: Noah
cast.who: The survivor of the flood, called Deucalion by Greeks.

cast.name: Epicurus
cast.who: Philosopher cited as an example of those who seemed happy in abundance and fame.

cast.name: Sardanapalus
cast.who: Legendary Assyrian king cited as an example of self-indulgent happiness.

cast.name: Heraclitus
cast.who: Early Greek philosopher cited as one hated and persecuted for living by reason.

cast.name: Musonius
cast.who: Roman Stoic philosopher cited as one hated and persecuted for living by reason.

cast.name: Pontius Pilate
cast.who: Roman governor under whom Jesus was crucified.

cast.name: Jesus Christ
cast.who: The Son of God, the whole Word, who became human for believers and to destroy demons.

voices.speaker: An unnamed person with tragic voice

key_terms.sense: A follower of Christ's teachings; the name for which people were condemned.
Fallen angels and their offspring who enslave humanity and cause persecution.
The divine Word or Reason, identified with Christ, present in whole in Christ and in seed in all people.
The seed of the Word implanted in all humanity, by which philosophers and lawgivers knew truth in part.
The eternal fire in which the unjust and demons will be punished.
Angels appointed by God to care for humanity, some of whom fell and fathered demons.
Free choice or deliberate will, by which each person does right or sins.
Fate or destiny, the Stoic doctrine Justin rejects.
Unbegotten, used of God the Father, who has no name because no one preceded him to give one.
The Roman bill of divorce by which the Christian woman separated from her husband.
The future destruction of the world by fire, which Justin says will happen by God's judgment, not Stoic transformation.
Philosophy, both human and divine; Justin calls Christianity the true and divine philosophy.
The seed or sowing of the Word in human nature, enabling partial knowledge of truth.
Confession, especially the public confession of being a Christian.

scripture: Justin uses the Septuagint (LXX) and refers to the prophets generally; he does not cite specific books by name in this work. When citing Old Testament books, use LXX book names and Psalm numbering, and note the modern equivalent where it differs (e.g., 1 Kingdoms = 1 Samuel).
uncertain: The exact date of composition is approximate.
The identity of the third Christian executed after Lucius is not given.
Whether the emperor or Senate ever published the work is unknown.
The bracketed sentence in section 15 about the Simonian teaching may be a later insertion.

_unresolved_facts.claim: including a Christian woman, Ptolemy, Lucius, and a third unnamed Christian
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὁ δὲ ταύτης ποτὲ ἀνήρ... πρὸς Πτολεμαῖόν τινα, ὃν Οὔρβικος ἐκαλέσατο... Καὶ τοῦ Οὐρβίκου κελεύσαντος αὐτὸν ἀπαχθῆναι, Λούκιός τις... καὶ ἄλλος δὲ τρίτος ἐπελθὼν κολασθῆναι προσετιμήθη
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Christian woman was accused but not executed; she petitioned the emperor and was granted leave to manage her affairs first. Ptolemy, Lucius, and a third unnamed Christian were executed under Urbicus.

_unresolved_facts.claim: to protest irrational persecution and to ask the Roman authorities to publish his defense so others may learn the truth
_unresolved_facts.fix: The request to publish appears only in sections 14-15, not in the stated occasion of section 1. The immediate occasion in section 1 is compelled by recent unjust actions under Urbicus and elsewhere.

_unresolved_facts.claim: a Christian woman who separated from her unchaste husband, leading to the condemnation of Ptolemy, Lucius, and a third Christian under Urbicus
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἡ μὲν βιβλίδιόν σοι τῷ αὐτοκράτορι ἀναδέδωκε... καὶ συνεχώρησας τοῦτο. Ὁ δὲ ταύτης ποτὲ ἀνήρ, πρὸς ἐκείνην μὲν μὴ δυνάμενος τανῦν ἔτι λέγειν, πρὸς Πτολεμαῖόν τινα... ἐτράπετο
_unresolved_facts.fix: The woman was not condemned; she successfully petitioned the emperor. The husband, unable to proceed against her further, turned against Ptolemy instead.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ['2'], move: 'He narrates the case of a Christian woman who separated from her unchaste husband; the husband first accused her of being a Christian, then turned against Ptolemy, her Christian teacher, leading to the executions of Ptolemy, Lucius, and a third Christian under Urbicus.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἡ μὲν βιβλίδιόν σοι τῷ αὐτοκράτορι ἀναδέδωκε... καὶ συνεχώρησας τοῦτο
_unresolved_facts.fix: The husband accused the wife of being a Christian, but she petitioned the emperor and was granted leave. The husband then turned against Ptolemy. The executions of Ptolemy, Lucius, and the third Christian occurred, but the woman was not among them.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ['8'], move: 'He expects to be plotted against, especially by Crescens, and challenges Crescens to a public examination.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Κἀγὼ οὖν προσδοκῶ ὑπό τινος τῶν ὠνομασμένων ἐπιβουλευθῆναι καὶ ξύλῳ ἐμπαγῆναι, ἢ κἂν ὑπὸ Κρίσκεντος... Καὶ γὰρ προσθέντα με καὶ ἐρωτήσαντα αὐτὸν ἐρωτήσεις τινὰς τοιαύτας... ἕτοιμος καὶ ἐφ᾽ ὑμῶν κοινωνεῖν τῶν ἐρωτήσεων πάλιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Justin says he has already questioned Crescens and exposed his ignorance, and is ready to do so again before the authorities. The challenge is to repeat questions already asked, not a new public examination.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections: ['12'], move: 'He recounts his own conversion from Platonism and refutes the slanders that Christians commit the crimes attributed to the gods.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ γὰρ αὐτὸς ἐγώ, τοῖς Πλάτωνος χαίρων διδάγμασι, διαβαλλομένους ἀκούων Χριστιανούς, ὁρῶν δὲ ἀφόβους πρὸς θάνατον... ἐνενόουν ἀδύνατον εἶναι ἐν κακίᾳ καὶ φιληδονίᾳ ὑπάρχειν αὐτούς
_unresolved_facts.fix: Justin recounts his thought process as a Platonist observing Christians, not his full conversion narrative. The section mainly refutes slanders and describes how demons extract false confessions through torture.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The centurion, who: 'A centurion, friend of the husband, who arrested and interrogated Ptolemy.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἑκατόνταρχον εἰς δεσμὰ ἐμβαλόντα τὸν Πτολεμαῖον, φίλον αὐτῷ ὑπάρχοντα, ἔπεισε λαβέσθαι τοῦ Πτολεμαίου καὶ ἀνερωτῆσαι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The centurion was a friend of the husband who had already put Ptolemy in bonds; the husband persuaded him to seize and interrogate Ptolemy. The centurion did not initiate the arrest but was persuaded to act.

_unresolved_facts.claim: speaker: 'Urbicus', how_marked: 'Direct speech introduced by ἔφη', sections: ['2']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ ὃς οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἀποκρινάμενος καὶ πρὸς τὸν Λούκιον ἔφη· Δοκεῖς μοι καὶ σὺ εἶναι τοιοῦτος
_unresolved_facts.fix: Urbicus speaks only one brief sentence (δοκεῖς μοι καὶ σὺ εἶναι τοιοῦτος), introduced by ἔφη but with the subject ὃς referring back to Urbicus through a complex sentence structure, not a simple 'Urbicus said' formula.

_unresolved_facts.claim: speaker: 'An unnamed person with tragic voice', how_marked: 'Direct speech introduced by ἀνεβόησεν', sections: ['12']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Εἴθε καὶ νῦν τις ἂν τραγικῇ φωνῇ ἀνεβόησεν ἐπί τι βῆμα ὑψηλὸν ἀναβάς· Αἰδέσθητε...
_unresolved_facts.fix: This is a wish/optative (εἴθε... ἀνεβόησεν), not an actual voice. Justin wishes someone would cry out with tragic voice, not that someone actually did.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: παρ᾿ ἡμῖν καλούμενον Νῶε, παρ᾿ ὑμῖν δὲ Δευκαλίωνα
_unresolved_facts.fix: Justin says Noah is called Deucalion 'by you' (Gentiles/Romans), not that Deucalion simply equals Noah. The relationship is presented as Greek equivalent name, not strict identity.
